translations.text: In the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh, the great city, in the days of Arphaxad, who ruled over the Medes in Ecbatana.
He built walls around Ecbatana with cut stones three cubits wide and six cubits long. He raised the wall to seventy cubits, and its width was fifty cubits.
He placed its towers over its gates, a hundred cubits high; the width of their foundations was sixty cubits.
He built its gates seventy cubits high and forty cubits wide, so that his army, its formations, his chariot officers, and the divisions of his infantry could march out.
In those days King Nebuchadnezzar fought a great war against King Arphaxad in the great plain in the territory of Ragau.

All those who lived in the hill country joined him, along with those who lived along the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Hydaspes, and in the plains of Arioch, king of the Elymeans. The nations came in a great and numerous battle formation against the descendants of Cheleul.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, sent for everyone living along the Euphrates, everyone living in Persia, everyone living in the west, those living in Cilicia, Damascus, Lebanon, and Anti-Lebanon, and everyone living facing the coast,
and the nations in Carmel, Gilead, Upper Galilee, and the great plain of Jezreel,
and everyone in Samaria and its cities, and along the bank of the Jordan as far as Jerusalem, Bethany, Chelous, and Kadesh, and the king of Egypt, Tahpanhes, Rameses, and all of Goshen,
as far as Tanis and Memphis, and everyone living in Egypt as far as the borders of Ethiopia.

But those living throughout the land scorned the command of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians. They did not join him in the war, because they were not afraid of him. Instead, in their eyes he was just one man. They sent his messengers back with contempt.

Nebuchadnezzar became angry with this whole land and swore by his royal throne, saying, “I will take revenge on the territory of Cilicia, Damascus, and Syria, and have my sword destroy them, along with everyone living in Moab, the Ammonites, all Judea, and everyone living in Egypt as far as the borders of the two seas.”
He deployed his army against King Arphaxad in the seventeenth year. He prevailed in battle and drove back all of Arphaxad’s army, his horses, and all his chariots.
He took control of his cities and pursued him as far as Ecbatana. He seized its towers and plundered its streets, leaving its splendor a heap of rubble.
He captured Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau, pierced him with his spears, and destroyed him utterly that day.
He returned there with his vast multitude of fighting men. He remained there, giving himself over to ease and pleasure, drinking wine with his multitude for a hundred and twenty days.

In the eighteenth year, on the twenty-second day of the first month, a decision was made in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, to take revenge on the whole earth, just as he had said.
He summoned all his servants and all his chief officials and shared the secret of his plan with them. With his own mouth he declared the full extent of the evil to be inflicted on the land.
They too decided to destroy every person who had not obeyed the command spoken by Nebuchadnezzar.
When his deliberations were finished, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, summoned Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of his army, who was second only to him, and said to him:
“This is what the great king, the lord of the whole earth, says: Look, come into my presence and take with you men of resolute heart.”
north of the plain near Dothan.

He told them to seize the mountain passes, because the road leading into Judea lay through them. It was easy to prevent anyone from passing through, since the approach was only wide enough for two men.
The Israelites did as Joakim the high priest and the elders of the whole people of Israel, who were residing in Jerusalem, had commanded them.
Everyone in Israel cried out to the Lord with earnest pleading, and they humbled themselves deeply.
They, their wives, their little children, their livestock, every foreign resident, their hired workers, and those they had bought with money put sackcloth around their waists.
Every man, woman, and little child living in Jerusalem fell down before the temple, scattered ashes on their heads, and spread out their sackcloth before the Lord.

They also covered the altar with sackcloth and cried out together to the God of Israel not to allow their little children to be carried off, their wives to be taken as plunder, the cities of their inheritance to be destroyed, or their holy places to be defiled and made a mockery for the nations to rejoice over.
The Lord heard their voices and saw their distress. All the people throughout Judea and Jerusalem were fasting with many cries before the Holy One, the Lord Almighty.

Joakim the high priest, every priest standing before the Lord, and those serving the Lord had sackcloth wrapped around their waists. They were offering the continual burnt offering, the offerings made in fulfillment of vows, and the offerings the people gave on their own behalf.
There were ashes on their turbans, and they cried out to the Lord with all their strength to look after the house of Israel with kindness.

Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of the Assyrian army, was told that the Israelites were preparing for war, that they had blocked the roads through the hill country, fortified all the peaks of the high mountain, and placed obstacles in the plains.
He became furiously angry and summoned all the rulers of Moab, the commanders of Ammon, and the governors of the coastal region.

He said to them, “Tell me, people of Canaan, who are these people who live in the hill country? What cities do they inhabit? How large is their army? What is the basis of their power and strength? Who has risen over them as king and leads their army?”
And why have they disobeyed by refusing to come to me, unlike all those living in the western regions?

Achior, the leader of all the Ammonites, said to him, “Let my lord hear a word from the mouth of your servant, and I will tell you the truth about these people who live in the hill country, dwelling [?]”
[?] the land of the Amorites, and they drove out all the people of Heshbon by their strength. They crossed the Jordan and took possession of the whole hill country.
They drove out before them the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, Shechem, and all the Girgashites, and they lived there for a long time.
As long as they did not sin before their God, good things were with them, because the God who hates injustice was with them.

But when they turned away from the way he had established for them, he swept them away in very many wars. They were taken captive to a land that was not theirs. The temple of their God became a bare patch of ground, and their cities were seized by their enemies.

Now that they have returned to their God, they have come back from the dispersion into which they were scattered. They have taken possession of Jerusalem, the place of their sanctuary, and settled in the hill country, because it was deserted.

Now then, lord, my lord, if there is ignorance among these people and they are sinning against their God, we will investigate them, because this will become a stumbling block among them. Then we will go up and fight against them.
But if there is no lawlessness in their nation, let the lord leave them alone, lest their Lord fight against them and their God attack them, and we become an object of mockery before the whole earth.
Now when Achior finished saying these words, he [?]
For his words will not prove empty.
But you, Achior, hireling of Ammon, who said these words on the day of your mistreatment, will not see my face again from this day until I punish the people who came out of Egypt.
Then the sword of my army and my servants will pass through your sides, and you will fall among their slain when I return.
My servants will take you back to the hill country and settle you in a house in the towns by the routes uphill.
You will not perish until they wipe you out along with them.
But if you hope in your heart that they will not be captured, do not let your face fall. I have spoken, and none of my words will fail.
Then Holofernes commanded his servants who were standing in his tent to seize Achior, take him back to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites.
His servants seized him and brought him out of the camp into the open country. They went up from the middle of the plain into the hill country and came to the springs below Bethulia.

When the men of the city who were on the mountain ridge saw them, they took up their weapons of war and came outside the city onto the mountain ridge. All the slingers blocked their way up and hurled stones at them.
They went down below the mountain, bound Achior, and left him tied up at the foot of the mountain. Then they went back to their master Holofernes.
The Israelites came down from their city, stood over him, and untied him. They brought him up to Bethulia and made him stand before the rulers of their city.
Those who held office in those days were Uzziah son of Micah, from the tribe of Simeon, Chabris son of Gothoniel, and Charmis son of Melchiel.

They summoned all the elders of the city, and all their children and their wives hurried together to the assembly. They made Achior stand in the midst of all their people, and Uzziah questioned him about what had happened.

He answered and told them what had been said at Holofernes’ assembly, all the words he himself had spoken among the rulers of the Assyrians, and the arrogant words Holofernes had spoken against the house of Israel.
The people bowed down and worshiped the Lord, and they cried out, saying:
“Lord, God of heaven, look down on their arrogance. Have mercy on the humiliation of our people, and look upon the faces of those who have humbled themselves before you today.”
They comforted Achior and honored him greatly.
Uzziah took him from the assembly to his house and prepared a great feast for the elders. Throughout that whole night they called on the God of Israel for help.
The next day Holofernes ordered his entire army and all the people who had come with him to the war to march out for battle [?].
[?] and all the leaders of the people of Moab and the commanders of the coastal region said:
Let our lord listen to a word, so that no defeat may occur among your forces.
For these people, the Israelites, do not put their trust in their spears, but in the height of the mountains, the mountains on which they live. For it is not easy to climb the peaks of the mountains.
So now, my lord, do not wage war against them as a battle is fought on the plain, and not a single man from your people will fall.
Remain in your camp, keeping every man in your army safe, and let your servants take control of the spring of water that flows out at the foot of the mountain.

For all the inhabitants of Bethulia draw water from that place. They will die of thirst and hand their city over to us. We and our people will climb the mountain peaks near them and remain there, keeping watch so that not a single person can come out of the city.
They will waste away before you, together with their wives and children. Before the sword comes down upon them, they will lie stretched out in the streets where they live.
Then you will repay them with a harsh punishment, because they have despised you and have not come out to meet you peacefully.
Their words pleased Holofernes and his servants, and he ordered them to do as they had said.
They [?]
in the passageways of their gates, and there was no longer any strength left in them.
All the people gathered around Uzziah and the rulers of the city, along with their young men and their little children. They cried out and said before all the elders:
May God judge between us immediately, for you have done us great wrong by not speaking peacefully with the Assyrians.
Now we have no helper, but our God has handed us over into their hands, to fall before them through thirst and severe hunger.
So now, call them and hand over the whole city as plunder to the people of Holofernes and his entire army.

For it is better for us to become their plunder. We will become their slaves, but our lives will be spared, and we will not see our little children die before our eyes, or our wives and children breathing their last.

We call heaven and earth, our God and the Lord of our ancestors, who punishes us according to our sins and the sins of our ancestors, to witness against you if you do not carry out these words this very day.
Then great weeping broke out throughout the entire assembly at once, and they cried out loudly to the Lord their God.
And Uzziah said to them, “Take courage, my brothers. Let us wait another five days, until the Lord our God turns his mercy toward us, for he will not abandon us completely.”
“But if these days pass and no help reaches us, we will do as you have said.”
He dismissed the people to their stations, and they went up onto the walls and towers of their city. They sent their wives and children home, and they were in great distress in the city.

In those days Judith heard about this. She was the daughter of Merari, son of Ox, son of Joseph, son of Uzziel, son of Elcia, son of Ananias, son of Gideon, son of Raphaim, son of Ahitub, son of Elijah, son of Hilkiah, son of Enab, son of Nathanael, son of Samael, son of Sarasadai, son of Israel.
Her husband was Manasseh, from her own tribe and family. He had died during the barley harvest.

For he had been standing over those who were binding the sheaves in the field when scorching heat struck his head. He lay down on his bed and died in Bethulia, his city. They buried him with his ancestors in the field between Dothan and Balamon.
Judith had been living in her house as a widow for three years and four months.
She had made herself a tent on the roof of her house and put sackcloth around her waist, and she wore the clothes of her widowhood.

She fasted throughout all the days of her widowhood, except on the days before the Sabbaths, the days before the new moons, the new moons themselves, the festivals, and the days of rejoicing of the house of Israel.

She had a very lovely face and was very beautiful in appearance. Her husband Manasseh had left her gold and silver, male and female slaves, livestock, and fields, and she remained in possession of them.
No one said anything evil against her, because she feared God greatly.

She heard the people's angry words against the ruler, because they had lost heart when their water supply dwindled. Judith also heard everything Uzziah had said to them, how he had sworn to them that he would hand the city over to the Assyrians after five days.
She sent her maid, who was in charge of her possessions, and summoned Chabris and Charmis, the elders of her city.

They came to her, and she said to them, “Listen to me, rulers of those who live in Bethulia. What you said before the people today is not right. You established the oath you uttered between yourselves and God, and you said you would hand the city over to our enemies if the Lord did not provide you with help within this time.
Now then, who are you to put God to the test today and set yourselves in God's place among human beings?
You have tried to examine the Lord Almighty, but you will never understand anything.

For you cannot fathom the depth of a human heart or express the thoughts within it. How, then, can you examine God, who made all these things, know his heart, and understand his thoughts? No, my brothers, do not provoke the Lord our God.
For if he does not wish to help us within the five days, he has the power to help us whenever he wishes, or to destroy us before our enemies.
“But you must not attempt to force the plans of the Lord our God, because God is not like a human being who can be threatened, nor like a mortal who can be brought to judgment.”
For we will call upon him to help us, while we wait for the salvation that comes from him, and he will listen to our voice if he wishes.
For no one has arisen in our generation, nor is there today any tribe, clan, community, or city among us that worships gods made by human hands, as happened in former days.
Because of this, our ancestors were handed over to the sword and to plundering, and they fell in a great slaughter before their enemies.
But we have known no other god besides him. Therefore we hope that he will not forget us or our people.
For if we are captured, all Judea will be devastated, and our sanctuary will be plundered. He will make us pay with our blood for their desecration.

He will bring the slaughter of our brothers, the captivity of the land, and the devastation of our inheritance back upon our heads among the nations where we will be slaves. We will become an object of reproach and ridicule before those who acquire us.
For our slavery will not turn out to be a blessing, but the Lord our God will make it a disgrace.
Now then, brothers, let us inform our brothers, because their lives depend on us, and the sanctuary and the house of their altar depend on us.
Besides all this, let us give thanks to the Lord our God, who tests us as he tested our ancestors.
Remember what he did to Abraham, the things through which he tested Isaac, and what happened to Jacob in Mesopotamia in Syria, while he was tending the sheep of Laban, his mother's brother.
For just as he tested them to examine their hearts, so with us too: he is not taking revenge on us. Rather, the Lord scourges those who are close to him to instruct them.”
Uzziah said to her, “Everything you have said, you have said with a good heart, and no one can oppose your words.
For your wisdom has not become apparent only today. From the earliest days, all the people have recognized your understanding, because the disposition of your heart is good.
But the people were terribly thirsty and forced us to do what we had told them. They also imposed an oath on us that we cannot break.
Now, then, pray for us, since you are a woman who worships God. The Lord will send rain and fill our cisterns, so that we will no longer perish.
Judith said to them, “Listen to me. I will do something that will become famous in the books of the descendants of our people.

You are to stand at the gate tonight, and I will go out with my maidservant. Within the days after which you said you would hand the city over to our enemies, the Lord will come to Israel’s aid through my hand.
But you must not question me about what I am doing, for I will not tell you until I have finished what I am going to do.”
Uzziah and the rulers said to her, “Go in peace, and may the Lord our God go before you to take vengeance on our enemies.”
Then they left the tent and went away to their assigned places.

Judith fell on her face, put ashes on her head, and exposed the sackcloth she was wearing. At the time when the evening incense was offered in Jerusalem, in the house of God, Judith cried out to the Lord and said in a loud voice:

“Lord, God of my father Simeon, you put a sword into his hand to take vengeance on the foreigners who broke open a virgin’s womb to disgrace it, exposed her thigh to shame her, and defiled her womb to dishonor her. For you said, ‘This must not happen,’ but they did it.

Because of this, you handed their rulers over to slaughter, and their bed, which was shamed by the deception with which they deceived her, [?] with blood. You struck down slaves along with rulers, and rulers on their thrones.

You gave their wives over to plunder, their daughters to captivity, and their possessions to be divided among the children of those you loved, who burned with your zeal, abhorred the defilement of their blood, and called upon you as their helper. God, my God, listen to me, a widow.
For you made what came before those events, those events themselves, and what came after them. You thought of the present and of what is to come, and what you had planned came into being.
The things you had determined stood ready and said, ‘Look, we are here.’ For all your ways are prepared, and your judgment is made with foreknowledge.

Look, the Assyrians have grown strong in their power. They have exalted themselves because of horse and rider, boasted of the multitude of their foot soldiers, and trusted in shield, spear, bow, and sling. They have not understood that you are the Lord who crushes wars.

The Lord is his name. Crush their strength and bring down their power in your anger, for they have planned to plunder your holy places, defile the resting place where the name of [?] dwells, and bring down the top of your altar with an axe.
Look down on their arrogance and send your wrath upon their heads. Give into my hand, a widow, the power I have planned for.
Through my deceptive words, strike down a slave along with a ruler, and a ruler along with his slave. Crush their pride by the hand of a woman.

For your power does not depend on great numbers, nor does your strength depend on mighty warriors. Rather, you are the God of the humble, the helper of the weak, the supporter of the feeble, the protector of the forgotten, and the savior of those who have no hope.
Yes, yes, God of my father and God of Israel’s inheritance, Lord of heaven and earth, creator of the waters of the rivers, king of all his creation, listen to my plea.
Make my words and my deception a wound and a blow to those who have planned cruel deeds against your covenant, your holy house, Mount Zion, and the house where your children find security.

And you will make yourself known throughout your whole nation and your whole tribe, so that they may know that you are God, the God of all power and the ruler, and that no one besides you protects the people of Israel.
When she had finished crying out to the God of Israel and had completed all these words,
she rose from the ground, called her maid, and went down to the place where she stayed on Sabbaths and during her festivals.

She removed the sackcloth she was wearing and took off her widow’s clothes. She washed her body with water, anointed herself with fine ointment, combed the hair of her head, put on a headdress, and dressed in her festive clothes, which she used to wear while her husband Manasseh was alive.
She put sandals on her feet and put on her anklets, bracelets, rings, earrings, and all her ornaments. She made herself very beautiful to attract the eyes of everyone who would see her.
She gave her maid a wineskin and a jar of oil, and filled a bag with flour, cakes of pressed fruit, and pure bread. She packed all her supplies and loaded them onto her maid.
They came to the gate of the city of Bethulia and found Uzziah standing there with the elders of the city, Chabris and Charmis.
When they saw her, with her appearance changed and her clothing different, they were utterly amazed at her beauty and said to her:
“May the God of our ancestors grant you favor and bring what you have undertaken to completion, for the pride of the children of Israel and the glory of Jerusalem.” And she worshiped God.
She said to them, “Give the order to open the city gate for me, so that I may go and carry out the things you discussed with me.” They ordered the guards to open it for her.

They did these things as they had said, and Judith went out with her maid. The men of the city watched her until she had descended the mountain and entered the valley, and they could no longer see her.
As she walked straight through the valley, the first Assyrian outpost met her.

They seized her and asked her, “To whom do you belong, and where have you come from?” She said, “I am a daughter of the Hebrews. I have fled from them because they are about to be given to you as prey.”

“I have come to meet Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of your army, to tell him the truth and show him a road by which he can go and take control of the entire hill country, without a single one of his men uttering a cry or a breath of life.”
When the men heard her words and looked at her face, her beauty caused them great amazement. They said to her,
“You have saved your life by hurrying down to meet our lord. Now go to his tent, and some of us will accompany you until they hand you over to him.”
“When you stand before him, do not be afraid in your heart. Speak to him, and he will treat you well.”
They selected a hundred men from among themselves and assigned them to escort her and her maid. They brought them to the tent of Holofernes.

People ran after one another throughout the whole camp, for news of her boldness had spread through all their quarters. They gathered around her as she stood outside Holofernes’ tent, until he was told about her.

They marveled at her beauty and, because of her, admired the daughters of Israel. Each said to the person beside him, “Who could despise this people, who have women like this among them? It is not good to leave even one of their men alive, since those who are left could deceive the whole world.”
Those who slept near Holofernes came out, along with all his servants, and brought her into the tent.
Holofernes was lying on his bed beneath his canopy, which was decorated with gold, silver, emeralds, and precious stones.
They told him about her, and he came out into the outer tent, with silver lamps carried before him.
When Judith came before him and his servants, they all marveled at the beauty of her face. She fell facedown and bowed before him, and his servants helped her up.

Holofernes said to her, “Take courage, woman. Do not be afraid in your heart, for I have never harmed anyone who was willing to serve Nebuchadnezzar, the king of the whole earth. For if it had not been
that your people who live in the hill country had insulted me, I would not have raised my spear against them. But they brought these things upon themselves.”
Now then, tell me why you fled from them and came to us. For you have come to safety. Take courage: you will live through this night and afterward.
For no one will harm you. Instead, they will treat you well, as they do the servants of my lord, King Nebuchadnezzar.
Judith said to him, “Listen to the words of your servant, and let your servant speak in your presence, for I will not lie to my lord tonight.”
And if you follow your servant’s words completely, God will accomplish something for you, and my lord will not fail in his undertakings.

For as Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth, lives, and as his power lives—the power by which he sent you to sustain every living being—not only human beings serve him because of you, but also the wild animals of the countryside, the livestock, and the birds of the sky. Through your strength, Nebuchadnezzar and his entire household will live.

For we have heard of your wisdom and the cleverness of your mind. These things have been reported throughout the earth: you alone are outstanding in every kingdom, powerful in your knowledge and mighty in matters of warfare.
Now, concerning the statement Achior made in your assembly, we have heard his words, because the people of Bethulia took him in, and he told them everything he had said before you.

Therefore, lord, my lord, do not disregard his statement, but keep it in your heart, because it is true. For our people cannot be punished, nor can a sword overpower them, unless they sin against their God.

So that my lord will not be turned back in his undertakings, do not take any action. Death will come upon them, and a sin has overtaken them through which they will provoke their God by doing things that are improper.

For their food has run out, and their water supplies have dwindled. They have decided what to do with their livestock, and they have planned to consume all the things that God, in his laws, set apart for them not to eat.

“They have decided to consume the firstfruits of the grain and the tithes of the wine and oil, which they had kept and consecrated for the priests who stand before our God in Jerusalem—things that no one among the people is permitted even to touch with their hands.”
They have also asked Jerusalem, because the others who live there have done these things, to have permission given to them through the elders.
And when an answer is given to them and they do these things, they will be handed over to you that very day for destruction.
For this reason, I, your servant, learned all these things and fled from their presence. God sent me to carry out with you deeds that will astonish everyone throughout the earth who hears of them.

For your servant worships God, serving the God of heaven day and night. So I will stay with you, my lord, and your servant will go out to the plain every night. I will pray to the God of heaven, and he will tell me when they have sinned.
Then I will come and tell you, and you will go out with your entire army, and none of them will stand against you.

I will lead you through the middle of Judea until you come to Jerusalem. I will set your throne in its midst, and you will lead them like sheep that have no shepherd. No dog will make a sound with its tongue in your presence. For these things were told to me and made known to me beforehand, and I was sent to tell them to you.
Her words pleased Holofernes and all his servants. They marveled at her wisdom and said:
“There is no woman like her from one end of the earth to the other, in the beauty of her face and the wisdom of her words.”
And Holofernes said to her, “God has done a good thing by sending you ahead of the people, so that you would come into our hands and those who insulted my lord would be seized and destroyed.”

“Now, you are beautiful in appearance and good in speech. If you act as you have said, their God will be my God, and you will live in the house of King Nebuchadnezzar and become famous throughout the earth.”
He ordered her to be taken into the place where his silver vessels were kept, and he said that she should be served some of the food prepared for him and drink some of his wine.
Judith said, “I will not eat any of it, so that it does not become a cause of offense. Instead, I will be supplied from the things I have brought with me.”
Holofernes said to her, “If the provisions you have with you run out, where will we get more to give you? For there is no one of your people here with us.”
Judith said to him, “As you live, my lord, your servant will not use up the provisions I have with me before I carry out with my own hand what I have planned.”
The servants of Holofernes brought her to the tent. She slept until midnight, then rose during the morning watch.
She sent word to Holofernes, saying, “Let my lord give orders to allow your servant to go out to pray.”
Holofernes ordered his guards not to prevent her. She stayed in the camp for three days, going out each night to the valley of Bethulia and bathing in the camp at the spring of water.
When she came up, she would plead with the God of Israel to make her way straight, so that the children of his people would be exalted.
When she came back in, she would remain purified in the tent until her food was brought to her in the evening.
On the fourth day, Holofernes held a feast for his servants alone and did not invite any of the officials in charge of affairs.
He said to Bagoas, his eunuch, who was in charge of all his possessions, “Go and persuade this Hebrew woman who is with you to come to us and eat and drink with us.
For it would be a disgrace to us if we let a woman like this go without speaking with her. If we do not win her over, they will laugh at us.”

Bagoas left Holofernes’s presence and went in to her. He said, “Let this beautiful young woman not hesitate to come to my lord and receive honor from him in the presence of those who belong to him. Drink wine with us and enjoy yourself, and today become like one of the daughters of the Assyrians who serve in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar.”
Judith said to him, “Who am I to refuse my lord? Whatever is pleasing in his eyes, I will hurry to do, and this will be a joy to me until the day of my death.”

She got up and adorned herself with her clothing and all her womanly finery. Her servant went ahead of her, and they spread rugs for her on the ground before Holofernes. These were the rugs they had received from Bagoas for the place where she stayed each day, so that she could recline on them while eating.

Judith went in and reclined. Holofernes’s heart was overwhelmed by her, and his soul was stirred, for he greatly desired to be with her. He had been looking for an opportunity to seduce her ever since the day he saw her.
Holofernes said to her, “Drink and enjoy yourself with us.”
Judith said, “I will drink, my lord, for today my life has been made greater than on any day since my birth.”
She took what her servant had prepared for her and ate and drank in his presence.
Holofernes was delighted with her and drank an enormous amount of wine, more than he had ever drunk in a single day since the day he was born.

When evening came, his servants hurried to retire. Bagoas closed the tent from outside, shutting out those who attended his lord. They went to their sleeping places, for they were all exhausted because the feast had been a great one.
Judith was left alone in the tent. Holofernes had already thrown himself onto his bed, for the wine had overcome him.

Judith had told her servant to stand outside her bedchamber and watch for her to come out as she did each day. For she had said, “I will go out to pray,” and she had spoken to Bagoas in the same terms.

They all went away, and no one, small or great, remained in the bedchamber. Judith stood beside his bed and said in her heart, “Lord, God of all power, look upon the work of my hands at this hour, so that Jerusalem may be exalted.
For now is the time to help your inheritance and to carry out what I have undertaken, to crush the enemies who have risen against us.”
She went to the bedpost at Holofernes’s head and drew his sword, which was there with him.
She approached his bed, grasped the hair of his head, and said, “Give me strength today, God of Israel.”
She struck him twice in the neck with all her strength and cut off his head.
She rolled his body off the bed, took the canopy down from the posts, and shortly afterward went out and gave Holofernes’ head to her maid.

She put it into the bag containing her food. The two of them went out together, as they usually did to pray. When they had passed through the camp, they went around that valley, climbed the mountain of Bethulia, and approached its gates.

Judith said to one of the guards at the gate, “Open! Open the gate! God is with us, our God! He will again perform a mighty deed in Israel and exercise his power against our enemies, as he has done today.”
When the people of her town heard her voice, they hurried down to the gate of their town and called all the elders of the town.

They all came running, from the least to the greatest, because her return seemed astonishing to them. They opened the gate and welcomed them, lit a fire to illuminate the place, and gathered around them.
She said to them in a loud voice, “Praise God! Praise, praise God, who has not withdrawn his mercy from the house of Israel, but has crushed the enemy by my hand this night!”

She took Holofernes’ head out of the bag and showed it to them. She said, “Here is the head of Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of the Assyrian army, and here is his canopy, which was spread over him in his tent. The Lord struck him down by the hand of a woman.
As the Lord lives, who protected me on the road I traveled, my face deceived him to his destruction, but he committed no sin with me to defile or shame me.”
All the people were utterly astonished. They fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying together, “Blessed are you, our God, who today have crushed the enemies of your people!”

Uzziah said to her, “My daughter, you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth, and blessed is the Lord God, who created the heavens and the earth, who guided you to cut off the head of the ruler of our enemies.
For your hope will never depart from the hearts of people as they remember the mighty deeds of God forever,

so that you may be rewarded with good things, because you did not spare your life in the face of our people’s humiliation, but went out amid our calamity, walking uprightly before God.” And all the people said, “May it be so! May it be so!”
Judith said to them, “Listen to me, my brothers. Take this head and hang it on the lookout post of your wall.

When dawn comes and the sun rises over the earth, let each of you take his weapons of war. Go outside the town, every able-bodied man, and put someone at your head, as though you were going down to the plain toward the first Assyrian outpost, and those who will go [?].

They will take their weapons and run to their camp, wake the commanders of the Assyrian army, and run together to Holofernes’ tent. They will not find him, and fear will fall upon them, and they will flee before you.
Then pursue them, you and everyone who lives in the territories of Israel, and strike them down along their roads.
But before you do these things, summon Achior the Ammonite for me, so that he may see and recognize the man who insulted the house of Israel and sent him to us as though to his death.”
They summoned Achior from Uzziah’s house. When he came and saw Holofernes’ head in the hand of a man in the assembly of the people, he fell on his face and fainted.

When he recovered, he threw himself at Judith’s feet and bowed before her. He said to her, “You are blessed [?] throughout the whole land of Judah and among every nation. When they hear your name, they will tremble.

Now, then, tell me what you have done [?] during these days.” Judith told him, in the midst of the people, everything she had done, from the day she went out until the moment she was speaking with them.
When she finished speaking, the people cheered loudly and raised a joyful shout in their city.
When Achior saw all these things that the Lord, the God of Israel, had done, he believed in God, circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and joined the house of Israel, to this very day.
When morning came, they hung Holofernes’ head outside the wall. Everyone took his weapons of war, and they went out in companies toward the approaches leading up the mountain.
When the Assyrians saw them, they sent for their leaders. These went to their generals, their commanders of thousands, and all their officers.
They came to Holofernes’ tent and said to the man who was in charge of all his belongings, “Wake our lord, because the Jews have dared to come down against us in battle, to wipe us out completely.”
Bagoas went inside and knocked at the entrance of the tent, for he thought that he was [?] sleeping with Judith.
When no one responded, he opened it and went into the bedroom. He found him sprawled on the couch, dead, with his head removed.
He cried out with a loud voice, with weeping, groaning, and a piercing cry, and tore his clothes.
He went into the tent where Judith had been, but did not find her. He ran out to the people and cried out.
“The slaves have acted treacherously! A woman from among the Hebrews has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar. Look, Holofernes is on the ground, and his head is no longer on him!”
When the officers of the Assyrian army heard these words, they [?] their clothes. They were deeply shaken and cried out with an exceedingly loud voice in the midst of the camp.
When those staying in their quarters heard, they were thrown into panic over what had happened.
Trembling and fear fell upon them, and no one waited for the person beside him. Instead, they were thrown into confusion all at once and fled along every road across the plain and the hill country.
Those encamped in the hill country and around Bethulia fled in disorder. Then the Israelites, every fighting man among them, rushed out against them.
Uzziah sent to Betomesthaim, Choba, Selbem, Cola, and every district of Israel to tell them what had happened, so that they would all rush out against those fighting them and kill them.

When the Israelites heard, they all came against them together and pursued them as far as Choba. Those from Jerusalem and from the whole hill country likewise came, for they had been told what had happened in their enemies’ camp. Those in Gilead and Galilee drove them away with great slaughter until they passed Damascus and its surrounding country.
The rest of those living in Bethulia fell upon the Assyrian camp, plundered it, and became very wealthy.

When the Israelites returned from the pursuit, they took possession of what remained. The villages and settlements in the hill country and the plain seized a great deal of plunder, for there was an exceedingly large quantity.
Joakim the high priest and the elders of the Israelites who lived in Jerusalem came to see the good things that the Lord had done for Israel, and to see Judith and speak with her in peace.
When they came to her, they all blessed her together and said to her, “You are the glory of Jerusalem! You are the great pride of Israel! You are the great pride of our people!

You have done all these things with your own hand. You have done good things for Israel, and God has been pleased with them. May you be blessed by the Lord Almighty forever.” And all the people said, “May it be so! May it be so!”

The people plundered the camp for thirty days. They gave Judith Holofernes’ tent, all his silver vessels, his couches, all his valuable possessions, and all his belongings. She took them and loaded them onto her mule. She also harnessed her wagons and loaded them onto those.
All the women of Israel ran together to see her. She formed a dancing group from among them. Branches were placed in her hands, and she gave them to the women who were with her.

She and those with her wore crowns of olive branches. She walked before all the people, leading the whole dancing group of women. All the men of Israel followed her, armed and wearing crowns, with praise on their lips.
Judith first recited this thanksgiving before all Israel. And when all the people repeated this praise,
Judith said, “Come before my God with tambourines. Sing to the Lord my God with cymbals. Sing a psalm to him, raise a song of praise, and call upon his name.
For the Lord is the God who crushes wars. He sent his armies into the midst of the people to rescue me from the hands of those pursuing me.
Assyria came from the mountains of the north. He came with the thousands of his forces, whose numbers were like rushing streams, and their horses covered the hills.
He said he would burn my territories, kill my young men with the sword, leave my nursing children on the ground, take my little daughters as plunder, and carry off my virgins.
The Lord Almighty defeated them by the hand of a woman.
For their mighty warrior did not fall at the hands of young men, nor was it the sons of the Titans who struck him down.
[?] nations that rise up against my people! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them on the day of judgment, putting fire and worms upon their flesh, and they will weep in pain forever.”
When they came to Jerusalem, they worshiped God. After the people had purified themselves, they offered their burnt offerings, their vowed offerings, and their gifts.
Judith dedicated to the Lord all the belongings of Holofernes that the people had given her, and the canopy she had taken from his bedroom.
The people remained in Jerusalem, rejoicing before the sanctuary for three months, and Judith stayed there.

After these days, each person went up to his inherited property. Judith also went up to his inherited property, and Judith went up to Bethulia. She remained on her estate and was honored throughout the whole land.
Many desired her, but no man had sexual relations with her throughout her life after the day her husband Manasseh died and was gathered to his people.

She continued to grow very great and grew old in her husband's house, reaching the age of one hundred and five years. She set her slave woman free. She died in Bethulia, and they buried her in the burial cave of her husband Manasseh.
The house of Israel mourned her for seven days. Before she died, she divided her possessions among all the relatives of her husband Manasseh and all her own relatives.
There was no one who troubled the Israelites throughout all the days of Judith, or for many days after her death.
